strengths: Addresses an underexplored and important problem: in-generation watermarking for autoregressive image generators, showing that direct transfer of red-green LLM watermarking fails due to VQ-VAE quantization/reconstruction mismatch and image perturbations.

Proposes a sensible cluster-based red-green watermarking framework, with a training-free variant and a perturbation-aware Cluster Classifier, clearly motivated by grouping similar tokens so that perturbations are more likely to preserve green/red assignment.

Extensive empirical study: three AR model settings (LlamaGen GPT-B, GPT-L, RAR-XL), multiple perturbations (JPEG, Gaussian noise/blur, salt-and-pepper, color jitter, regeneration attacks), ablations over number of clusters, penalty, green fraction, and prefix, plus FID and verification runtime.

Results support the main claims: cluster-based watermarking improves robustness over the naive token-level method, and +CC further boosts detection (e.g., GPT-B Salt&Pepper .1 TPR@FPR=1% improves from 0.161 for No Clustering to 0.999 for +CC; RAR-XL improves from 0.138 to 0.998), while FID remains reasonably close to baselines and verification is fast.
The paper is clearly written, includes detailed experimental settings, perturbation definitions, hyperparameters, and a code-release statement, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is moderate: the core idea of clustering similar tokens is intuitive and closely related to semantic watermarking for LLMs and concurrent token-level AR watermarking; the contribution is mainly an adaptation/extension rather than a fundamentally new watermarking paradigm.

The detection statistic uses a Binomial(T, γ) null, but green clusters are selected by count (k_green = floor(γk)) without accounting for unequal cluster sizes or token frequencies. The actual green-token fraction under the null can deviate from γ, potentially miscalibrating p-values and FPR; this is not validated in the paper.

Main results report the best-performing hash prefix selected via perturbation Set A, then evaluate on the stronger Set B. Although not direct test leakage, this is a robustness-tuned hyperparameter, and average-over-prefix results are only reported for Set A, not for the main Set B, making the headline numbers potentially optimistic.
Evaluation is limited to ImageNet class-to-image AR models; no text-to-image AR setting is tested, and the concurrent IndexMark comparison is only on LlamaGen GPT-B, not GPT-L or RAR-XL.

Robustness limitations remain: training-free clustering still performs poorly under blur and salt-and-pepper noise, and geometric transformations are not evaluated. The +CC improvement depends on training with perturbation augmentations.
FID increases are non-negligible for RAR-XL (3.13 to 3.96), so the claim of preserving image quality may be somewhat overstated; no perceptual or user study is provided.

The Cluster Classifier integration at verification time is somewhat underspecified (token vs. cluster prediction), and no direct comparison is provided to concurrent token-reconstruction watermarking methods such as Jovanović et al.

strengths: The paper identifies a concrete and well-motivated problem: naive red-green (Kirchenbauer-style) token-level watermarking transfers poorly to AR image generators because VQ-VAE encoding/decoding is not perfectly invertible and small perturbations move latents across codebook entries, breaking the token-level green set assignment. This diagnosis (Section 3.2, Figure 5) is clear and empirically supported.

The proposed remedy—assigning entire clusters of similar codebook tokens to green/red sets—is simple, intuitive, and directly addresses the identified failure mode. The training-free clustering variant is appealing since it requires no finetuning and preserves image quality (FID comparable to no-watermark).

The evaluation is broad and thorough: two AR models (LlamaGen GPT-B/GPT-L, RAR-XL), multiple image resolutions, two perturbation sets, regeneration attacks (SD1.5-AE, FLUX.1-AE, SD2.1-Regeneration), and ablation over the number of clusters k, penalty δ, green fraction γ, and hash prefix. The supplementary tables (7–9) and ablations (Figures 3, 4, 7, 8) give strong support for the main claims.

Results show consistent and often large robustness gains over the training-free baseline and over strong post-hoc baselines (DWT-DCT, DWT-DCT-SVD, RivaGAN) as well as the concurrent IndexMark, especially for salt-and-pepper noise, color jitter, and regeneration, while retaining low FID.

The verification runtime analysis (Table 2) is a useful practical contribution: token-based verification is orders of magnitude cheaper than inversion-based diffusion watermarking (e.g., Tree-Ring), which is a genuine advantage for deployment.
The paper is clearly written, the method and algorithm (Algorithm 1) are easy to follow, and the authors commit to releasing code, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty relative to concurrent work is limited. The paper itself notes several concurrent token-level AR watermarking works (Tong et al./IndexMark, Jovanović et al., Wu et al.). The core idea of grouping similar tokens/clusters is closely related to semantic watermarking for LLMs (Ren et al.), and Jovanović et al. also train a perturbation-aware token reconstruction model. The distinction (predicting clusters vs. reconstructing tokens) is real but incremental; the framing as 'among the first' slightly overstates the conceptual advance given this concurrent landscape.

The hash-prefix tuning procedure raises a fairness/overfitting concern: the best prefix is selected by 'averaging all TPR values and choosing the best performing prefix' on the same perturbation sets used to report the main results. This selection-on-evaluation-data can inflate the reported numbers, and the variance across prefixes (Figure 5) is large for small k, so the gains may partly reflect favorable prefix choice rather than intrinsic robustness. A held-out prefix selection protocol would be more convincing.

Robustness is still weak in the cases that matter most: Gaussian blur and (for some settings) salt-and-pepper remain difficult, with the training-free variant dropping to 14–52% TPR@1%FPR and the blur column being the only perturbation where the method does not clearly beat baselines. Geometric transformations (rotation, zoom, crop) are explicitly acknowledged as unaddressed, which limits real-world applicability.

The stronger variant (+ CC) requires finetuning the VAE encoder for 30 epochs on 100k generated images (~12h on an A40) and depends on a perturbation schedule (Table 6). This weakens the 'training-free/simple' selling point for the best-performing configuration, and the comparison against fully post-hoc baselines is not apples-to-apples since the method requires access to the generation process and codebook.

Some comparisons are incomplete: IndexMark is only evaluated on LlamaGen and not on RAR-XL, and no direct head-to-head on RAR-XL against the concurrent token-level methods is provided, so the claim of beating 'all baselines' is only partially supported across models.

The paper does not evaluate watermark removal/security attacks beyond regeneration (e.g., adversarial or learned removal, or the Zhao et al. attack with stronger settings), so the robustness claim is scoped to a particular (albeit reasonable) perturbation suite. Detection thresholds and false-positive behavior under distribution shift of the codebook/clusters are also not stress-tested.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: watermarking autoregressive (AR) image generators, which has received less attention than diffusion-model watermarking.

Proposes a clear and reasonable adaptation of red-green watermarking to AR image models via visual token clustering, with two variants: a training-free cluster-based method and a fine-tuned Cluster Classifier.

Provides an extensive empirical study across three AR models (LlamaGen GPT-B, GPT-L, RAR-XL), multiple perturbations, regeneration attacks, and ablations over number of clusters, penalty, green fraction, and hash prefix.

The Cluster Classifier variant achieves strong TPR@FPR=1% under many perturbations, often outperforming post-hoc baselines (DWT-DCT, DWT-DCT-SVD, RivaGAN) and the concurrent IndexMark method on LlamaGen GPT-B.
Verification runtime is comparable to lightweight post-hoc watermarking, and the authors promise code release for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The main results are optimistically biased because the best hash prefix (and likely other hyperparameters) is selected using the same 2,000 watermarked and 2,000 unwatermarked test images used for final evaluation; the supplement shows prefix variance, so average performance is likely lower than reported.

Technical novelty is limited relative to concurrent work: several recent papers already explore token-level or clustering-based watermarking for AR image generation, and the proposed cluster-level red-green scheme is an incremental adaptation; comparison to concurrent AR watermarking is restricted to IndexMark on one model, with no comparison on GPT-L or RAR-XL.

The training-free cluster variant still fails under strong perturbations such as Gaussian noise, blur, and salt-and-pepper noise; the robust +CC variant relies on fine-tuning with the same perturbation families used in evaluation, weakening evidence for generalization to unseen attacks.

Regeneration attack results are surprisingly high (e.g., >0.99 TPR) and are not analyzed; attack strength and parameters (e.g., SD2.1-Regeneration denoising strength) are not fully specified, raising reproducibility and potential weak-attack concerns.

The p-value computation assumes a Binomial(T, γ) null, but the cluster-level green set size may not equal γ|V| because clusters have unequal sizes, which can miscalibrate detection thresholds and affect reported ROC/AUC.

Robustness to geometric transformations (rotation, zoom) is not evaluated, and the paper acknowledges token-based watermarking is not robust to such spatial misalignments, limiting the scope of the robustness claims.
Image quality is degraded relative to unwatermarked baselines (e.g., FID increases from 3.13 to 3.96 on RAR-XL), and the trade-off is not deeply analyzed.

strengths: Addresses the underexplored problem of watermarking autoregressive image generators, extending KGW-style token watermarking to visual token sequences and identifying the token-reconstruction brittleness under image perturbations.

Proposes a simple but effective cluster-based watermarking scheme: clustering the VQ-VAE codebook and assigning whole clusters to green/red sets improves robustness against perturbations while preserving generation quality.

Provides two practical variants: a training-free clustering approach and a training-based extension with token/cluster classifiers fine-tuned on perturbation-augmented data, giving flexibility for different deployment settings.

Conducts extensive experiments on multiple AR image models (LlamaGen GPT-B/GPT-L and RAR-XL) across a wide range of perturbations, regeneration attacks, and geometric transformations, with comparisons to post-hoc and concurrent in-generation watermarking baselines.

Reports strong empirical results: clustering substantially improves TPR@FPR=1% and AUC, classifier variants further boost robustness, FID/CLIP remain close to unwatermarked generation at k=64, and verification runtime is lightweight.

Includes useful ablations on number of clusters, watermark strength, green-token fraction, hash prefix selection, cluster initialization, and SyncSeal-based geometric synchronization, with detailed supplementary material.
Reproducibility is supported by clear algorithmic descriptions, model/perturbation settings, and stated availability of code and implementation details.
weaknesses: The core method is a relatively straightforward combination of KGW-style watermarking with k-means clustering of the visual codebook; novelty is moderate and there is no theoretical analysis of detection reliability, false-positive control, or security guarantees.
Evaluation is limited to class-conditional ImageNet generation on three AR models; no results on text-to-image or open-ended AR generators, and no user study or broader deployment evaluation.

The security evaluation is largely qualitative. The paper assumes a trusted API setting and does not empirically test watermark removal, forgery, spoofing, or adaptive attacks, which are important for a watermarking method.

Verification depends on access to the VQ-VAE encoder/quantizer or a private model/API to reconstruct tokens or clusters; this limits applicability in purely post-hoc or black-box settings and is only partially discussed.

The green-cluster assignment uses a fixed number of green clusters, but cluster sizes may be unbalanced; the binomial p-value assumes a green fraction of gamma, while the actual green token probability may deviate. Prefix tuning mitigates this heuristically but introduces validation-set selection and possible overfitting/security concerns.

Some comparisons are incomplete: WMAR is not evaluated on LlamaGen, and the set of concurrent AR watermarking baselines remains limited; broader comparison to additional in-generation AR watermarking methods would strengthen the claims.

The token/cluster classifier variants require training on 100k generated images and are model-specific, adding training cost and reducing the simplicity of the training-free variant; this trade-off is not fully analyzed.
Even the best method still struggles under strong Gaussian blur and salt-and-pepper noise, so the robustness claim is qualified, and the abstract/source-code URL appears incomplete in the manuscript.

strengths: Addresses an under-explored yet practically important problem: in-generation watermarking for autoregressive (AR) image generators, which have received far less attention than diffusion-model watermarking despite rapid adoption of AR image models.

Clear and well-motivated technical narrative: the authors correctly diagnose why a naive KGW-style token-level watermark fails for AR image models (token reconstruction mismatch through the VQ-VAE encode/decode and amplification by image perturbations), and propose a principled fix—clustering semantically/geometrically similar codebook tokens so that red/green assignment is stable to perturbations.

Two practical variants are offered: a training-free cluster-based approach that only modifies sampling, and a fine-tuned token/cluster classifier that further improves robustness—giving the method flexibility depending on deployment constraints.

Extensive empirical evaluation: three AR models (LlamaGen GPT-B/GPT-L, RAR-XL), a broad perturbation suite (JPEG, Gaussian noise/blur, salt & pepper, color jitter, regeneration via SD1.5-AE/FLUX.1-AE/SD2.1), and large-scale image generation (~5M images). Ablations over cluster count k, penalty δ, green-token fraction γ, and hash prefix κ are thorough.

Strong reported robustness improvements over post-hoc baselines (DWT-DCT-SVD, RivaGAN, TrustMark, SSL) and concurrent AR methods (IndexMark, WMAR) across most perturbations, with only a modest FID increase and preserved CLIP scores.
Competitive verification runtime (10–25 ms), which is a meaningful practical advantage over diffusion-model in-generation watermarking methods that require full inversion.

Honest reporting of limitations, including failure on geometric transformations and the empirical prefix-tuning heuristic; the addition of SyncSeal-based results (Tables 9–10) partially addresses this and shows near-100% TPR after synchronization.
Good reproducibility signals: detailed experimental setup, perturbation sets A/B, training details, computing infrastructure, and released source code.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate/incremental: the core idea of clustering semantically similar tokens and sharing red/green assignment is closely related to existing semantic watermarking for LLMs (e.g., Ren et al. 2024) and concurrent AR image watermarking work (Wu et al. 2025; Tong et al. IndexMark). The paper positions itself as 'among the first' but the conceptual leap is limited to transferring this idea to VQ-VAE-based AR image models.

The reported gains are largest against post-hoc watermarking baselines, which are known to be weak under in-generation threat models. The comparison to genuinely relevant concurrent work (IndexMark, WMAR) is smaller and limited to available-code models, so the headline 'state-of-the-art' claim is somewhat qualified.

Prefix tuning (Sec. 3.4) is an ad-hoc empirical selection over κ ∈ {1..8} with no theoretical justification. The authors acknowledge this is a heuristic and it introduces a security concern (narrowing the effective key space), which is only partly mitigated by the argument that a real deployment would draw from a larger space.

Robustness to salt & pepper noise and blurring still degrades notably without the fine-tuned classifier, and geometric transformations (rotation, cropping, scaling, flipping) essentially destroy the watermark out-of-the-box; recovery depends on an external synchronization layer (SyncSeal), which somewhat weakens the standalone robustness story.

FID degrades noticeably at low cluster counts (k ≤ 8), and the best hyperparameters (k=64, δ=5, γ=0.25) are tuned on a validation set; sensitivity of results to these choices and to prefix selection may not transfer cleanly to new models or distributions.

The security analysis (Supp. D) assumes the model/VQ-VAE/classifier are private, which is standard, but the threat model against adversarial removal is only briefly discussed and not empirically tested beyond regeneration-style attacks.

Some claims would benefit from clearer statistical grounding—e.g., variance across prefixes is shown but the selection of the 'best' prefix on the test distribution risks optimistic bias, even though the authors state a held-out test set is used.

strengths: Correct and useful diagnosis of why naive KGW transfer fails for AR image generators: VQ-VAE quantization is unstable, so small perturbations move latent codes to different codebook tokens, breaking the token-level green/red partition. This is a clear, well-motivated observation.

The cluster-based remedy is simple, training-free, and empirically effective. For LlamaGen GPT-B, TPR@FPR=1% under Gaussian blur R3 rises from 0.068 (no clustering) to 0.663, and under salt & pepper from 0.069 to 0.402, and clustering alone substantially beats IndexMark on most perturbations (e.g., JPEG 0.956 vs 0.821; blur R3 0.663 vs 0.171).

Broad empirical study: three AR models (LlamaGen GPT-B/GPT-L, RAR-XL), a wide perturbation suite, ablations over cluster count k, penalty δ, green fraction γ and hash prefix, FID/CLIP analysis, cluster-initialization variance, and geometric-transform robustness with SyncSeal. The ~5M generated images and released code support reproducibility.
Verification runtime is lightweight (comparable to DWT-DCT-SVD/RivaGAN), a genuine practical advantage over inversion-based diffusion watermarking.
Honest reporting of failure modes (blur and strong salt-and-pepper remain hard for the training-free variant) and a thoughtful security discussion.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The green/red token-partitioning idea is inherited from KGW; the clustering is concurrent with Wu et al. [39] (clustering-based AR watermarking) and conceptually close to IndexMark [33], which pairs similar tokens (albeit assigning them to opposite sets). The paper itself concedes this overlap, so the delta (same-cluster assignment, training-free variant) is incremental rather than a new framework.

The headline numbers in Table 1 largely come from the '+ Token Classifier' / '+ Cluster Classifier' variants, which require fine-tuning on 100k generated images (~12h on an A40) and are explicitly acknowledged to resemble the trained token reconstructors of IndexMark and WMaR. Thus the strongest results rely on components that are not novel, and the training-free variant alone is competitive with, but not clearly superior to, WMaR on Gaussian perturbations.

Prefix tuning (choosing κ from 8 candidates on a validation set) is an ad-hoc heuristic that shrinks the effective key space; the justification (Fig. 5) is qualitative, and the paper defers better solutions to future work. This leaves an unexplained dependence of robustness on a secret whose selection is essentially fit to the evaluation.

Evaluation is confined to class-conditional ImageNet AR models at 256/384 resolution; no text-to-image AR generators (e.g., Emu-3, text-conditioned VAR) are tested, and comparison against concurrent AR watermarking covers only IndexMark and WMaR, weakening the generality of the 'state-of-the-art' claim.

Robustness is argued in part on very destructive perturbations (Gaussian blur R=3, S&P 0.1) that the paper itself notes severely degrade image quality, so the practical significance of those particular numbers is limited; detection is also only characterized at a single FPR operating point, with little analysis of false-positive behavior on out-of-distribution images.

No evaluation of removal/forgery attacks beyond the standard 'keep the model private' assumption; given that the watermark is defined by a public statistical test and a learned classifier, adversarial robustness of the scheme is not demonstrated.
